possible_confounders: Sensor placement variability across subjects (e.g., wrist vs. chest, tightness)
Body composition differences (BMI, adiposity) affecting signal quality
Age-related vascular stiffness differences not captured by HRV
Medication use (beta-blockers, antihypertensives) altering autonomic readings
control_variables: Standardized sensor placement protocol
BMI, age, sex as covariates in conformal predictor
Medication logs and exclusion criteria
Within-subject normalization of HRV metrics
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage instability stems from systematic sensor placement differences across subjects, not autonomic physiology
Body composition (adiposity) attenuates PPG/ECG amplitude, increasing residual variance independent of autonomic state
Age-related arterial stiffening changes pulse wave morphology, causing model misspecification that mimics autonomic heterogeneity
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If sensor placement or body composition drives coverage deviation, then coverage will correlate with signal amplitude/quality metrics (e.g., PPG AC/DC ratio) rather than autonomic parameters (RMSSD, BRS) after controlling for subject ID.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a multivariate regression of per-subject coverage deviation on both autonomic parameters (RMSSD, LF/HF) and signal quality metrics (PPG SNR, AC/DC ratio), the signal quality metrics remain significant predictors (p < 0.01) while autonomic parameters become non-significant (p > 0.05).
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires simultaneous measurement of autonomic markers and signal quality indices per subject per segment. Testable by re-analyzing existing multi-subject datasets with added signal quality covariates.

possible_confounders: Physiological state changes co-occurring with motion (e.g., stress increases both movement and HRV)
Electrode impedance changes due to sweating (physiological) vs. mechanical loosening (artifact)
Skin temperature changes affecting both impedance and vascular tone
Circadian variation in baseline impedance independent of motion
control_variables: Simultaneous reference ECG/PPG with gel electrodes as ground truth
Skin temperature and sweat rate monitoring
Controlled motion protocols (treadmill, arm movements) at fixed physiological states
Impedance spectroscopy at multiple frequencies to separate contact vs. tissue effects
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage drops during high-motion segments because physiological dynamics genuinely change (e.g., HRV suppression during exercise), not because sensor noise corrupts measurements
Sweating reduces electrode impedance and improves contact, counteracting motion artifacts; net effect on coverage is non-monotonic
Impedance drift correlates with recording duration (gel drying), which also correlates with circadian phase, creating spurious motion-artifact association
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If physiological state changes drive coverage failure, then segments with matched motion levels but different physiological states (e.g., stress vs. exercise at same accelerometer variance) will show different coverage; if sensor noise drives it, coverage will depend only on motion/impedance metrics regardless of physiological state.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a controlled protocol where subjects perform matched-motion tasks at different physiological arousal levels (e.g., mental stress vs. physical exercise at same accelerometer RMS), coverage deviation correlates with physiological state markers (e.g., cortisol, HRV) after adjusting for motion metrics (p < 0.01 for state, p > 0.05 for motion).
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires disentangling motion artifact from true physiological non-stationarity. Best tested with simultaneous reference-grade and wearable sensors during controlled state manipulations.

possible_confounders: Movement artifacts coinciding with state transitions (e.g., body movements during arousals)
Signal quality degradation during transitions (e.g., electrode displacement during posture change)
Circadian modulation of state transition frequency and duration
Medication effects on sleep architecture and transition dynamics
control_variables: Accelerometer-derived movement intensity during transitions
Signal quality indices (SQI) per 30-sec epoch
Time-of-day and circadian phase as covariates
Medication status and timing
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage drops at state transitions because movement artifacts corrupt the signal during transitions (e.g., body movements during arousals), not because autonomic dynamics change
Transitions involve brief signal quality drops (electrode displacement, sensor motion) that bias conformity scores, mimicking distributional shifts
The apparent transition effect is confounded by circadian phase: transitions cluster at certain phases where coverage is worse for independent reasons
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If movement artifacts drive coverage drops, then coverage will correlate with movement intensity during transition windows regardless of state type; if autonomic shifts drive it, coverage will correlate with autonomic markers (HRV complexity, RSA) after controlling for movement.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In segments with verified state transitions (PSG-scored) but low movement (accelerometer variance < 10th percentile), coverage still drops ≥ 10% post-transition; conversely, high-movement periods without state transitions show no coverage drop.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires high-resolution PSG + accelerometer + physiological signals. Testable by stratifying transitions by movement intensity and measuring coverage recovery dynamics.

possible_confounders: Daily activity/sleep patterns (behavioral) driving both circadian phase and signal characteristics
Environmental temperature cycles affecting both skin temperature and sensor performance
Mealtimes and metabolic cycles influencing physiology and signal quality
Light exposure patterns affecting both circadian phase and activity
control_variables: Continuous actigraphy and light exposure monitoring
Ambient and skin temperature logging
Meal timing and composition logs
Forced desynchrony or constant routine protocol data (gold standard)
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage oscillates because daily activity patterns (sleep/wake, exercise) create non-stationarity, not endogenous circadian rhythms
Environmental temperature cycles cause sensor drift (e.g., PPG baseline wander) that mimics circadian residual shifts
Postprandial hemodynamic changes after meals create periodic residual shifts aligned with mealtimes, not circadian phase
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If behavioral/environmental cycles drive coverage oscillation, then coverage rhythm will persist in constant routine conditions (constant posture, dim light, hourly snacks) but with altered phase/amplitude; if endogenous circadian drives it, rhythm will free-run with ~24.2h period in constant routine.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a constant routine protocol (≥ 40h), coverage oscillation persists with a period significantly different from 24h (e.g., 24.2 ± 0.5h) and phase-locks to DLMO, not clock time; in normal conditions, coverage oscillation phase-locks to clock time/activity.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Gold standard test requires constant routine or forced desynchrony data. In observational data, use structural equation modeling to separate endogenous vs. exogenous rhythmic components.

possible_confounders: True physiological variability in ambiguous segments (e.g., N1/N2 boundary) that raters disagree on because physiology is genuinely intermediate
Signal quality degradation causing both labeling difficulty and prediction difficulty
Rater fatigue/drift correlating with recording duration or time-of-day
Systematic scoring differences between labs/scorers unrelated to signal characteristics
control_variables: Signal quality index (SQI) per segment
Physiological ambiguity metrics (e.g., entropy, spectral boundary features)
Rater identity, experience, and time-on-task
Adjudicated consensus labels as ground truth reference
boring_rival_explanations: Low inter-rater agreement marks segments where physiology is genuinely ambiguous (transitional states), and the model correctly reflects this uncertainty; conformal coverage appears off because the 'true' label is undefined
Poor signal quality causes both labeling disagreement and prediction errors; label noise is a proxy for signal quality, not an independent confounder
Rater drift over time creates artificial segment-dependent noise that correlates with recording session, not physiology
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If true physiological ambiguity drives coverage deviation, then segments with low rater agreement but high signal quality will show symmetric coverage errors (both over/under); if label noise drives it, coverage errors will correlate with rater-specific biases (e.g., systematic over-scoring of N3) after controlling for SQI.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: Using adjudicated labels as ground truth, segments with high initial disagreement (kappa < 0.6) but high SQI show coverage within 2% of nominal when calibrated on adjudicated labels; segments with low SQI show coverage deviation > 8% even with adjudicated labels.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires multi-rater annotated data with adjudication. Testable by simulating label noise at known rates vs. selecting genuinely ambiguous segments via physiological features.

possible_confounders: Motion artifacts during exercise corrupting sensor signals (confounded with activity)
Hemodynamic changes (BP, vascular tone) during exercise altering signal morphology independent of autonomic dynamics
Sensor displacement during vigorous activity changing optical path / electrode contact
Sweating altering electrode impedance and PPG baseline
control_variables: Reference-grade signals (arterial line, cuff BP) during controlled exercise protocols
Accelerometer-derived motion artifact metrics (frequency-domain separation)
Skin temperature and sweat rate
Sensor contact force/pressure monitoring (if available)
boring_rival_explanations: Undercoverage during exercise is caused by motion artifacts corrupting the PPG/ECG waveform, not by genuine cardiovascular dynamics changes
Sensor displacement during movement changes the measurement geometry, creating apparent residual shifts that are measurement artifacts
Sweating reduces electrode impedance, changing noise characteristics in a way that mimics physiological non-stationarity
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If motion artifacts drive undercoverage, then coverage during exercise will correlate with motion artifact metrics (accelerometer high-frequency power) after controlling for activity intensity (METs); if cardiovascular dynamics drive it, coverage will correlate with hemodynamic markers (pulse transit time, BP variability) after controlling for motion.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a controlled exercise protocol with simultaneous reference BP and wearable PPG, segments matched on METs but differing in motion artifact severity (e.g., cycling vs. running at same METs) show coverage deviation tracking motion metrics (p < 0.01) not METs (p > 0.05).
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Critical to separate motion artifact from true physiological non-stationarity. Best tested with reference hemodynamics during controlled activities with different motion profiles at matched intensity.

possible_confounders: Measured covariates that are imperfect proxies for the true confounders (e.g., self-reported medication adherence vs. actual plasma levels)
Time-varying measured covariates not included in the model (e.g., posture, recent food intake)
Selection bias: segments with certain confounder values are more likely to be recorded
Carryover effects from prior segments (e.g., medication half-life, hydration persistence)
control_variables: Objective confounder measures: plasma drug levels, urine specific gravity, salivary caffeine
High-frequency posture/activity monitoring
Segment sequencing and temporal dependency modeling
Sensitivity analysis parameters (Rosenbaum Γ bounds)
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage variation is explained by measured covariates that were omitted from the conformal predictor (e.g., posture, recent caffeine), not by unmeasured confounders
The apparent confounder effect is actually selection bias: segments with extreme confounder values are underrepresented in calibration
Temporal autocorrelation in residuals creates spurious segment-wise coverage variation that mimics confounding
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If measured but omitted covariates drive coverage variation, then adding them to the conformal predictor (as stratification or covariates) will eliminate the coverage-confounder correlation; if truly unmeasured confounders drive it, coverage variation will persist even after adjusting for all measured covariates, and sensitivity analysis will require large Γ to explain away.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with gold-standard confounder measures (plasma drug levels, urine osmolarity), adding these to the conformal framework reduces coverage-confounder correlation to non-significance (p > 0.05) and brings conditional coverage within 2% of nominal across confounder strata.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires dataset with measured putative confounders. Testable via sequential addition of confounder proxies to conformal predictor and Rosenbaum sensitivity analysis on residual coverage variation.

possible_confounders: Physiological state changes causing both missingness and signal changes (e.g., arrhythmia causing both dropout and HRV changes)
Device-specific firmware/algorithm differences affecting both sampling and signal processing
Battery voltage drops causing both reduced sampling and sensor performance degradation
Environmental interference (EMI) causing both packet loss and signal corruption
control_variables: Device firmware version and hardware revision
Battery voltage logging
EMI environment monitoring (if feasible)
Simultaneous reference sensor with wired connection
boring_rival_explanations: Missing data is a symptom of physiological events (e.g., arrhythmia, movement) that also change the signal distribution; the missingness mechanism is not the cause
Device firmware updates change both sampling behavior and signal processing, creating apparent missingness effects that are actually software version effects
Low battery reduces both transmission rate and sensor drive current, degrading signal quality independently of missing data pattern
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If physiological events drive both missingness and coverage failure, then segments with artificially induced MCAR missingness (simulated dropout) will maintain nominal coverage, while segments with physiologically correlated missingness will not; if missingness mechanism itself drives it, MCAR missingness will also degrade coverage.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with simultaneous wired reference and wireless wearable, artificially imposing MCAR missingness (random dropout) on the wireless stream at 30% rate yields coverage within 3% of nominal, while the native MNAR missingness at same rate yields coverage deviation > 10%.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Testable by controlled missingness injection experiments on complete datasets with known ground truth. Requires distinguishing missingness mechanism from physiological correlates.

possible_confounders: Segment length correlates with physiological state (e.g., short segments during transitions, long during stable sleep)
Segment length correlates with signal quality (e.g., event-triggered recordings stop when signal degrades)
Model complexity interacts with segment-specific non-stationarity, not just sample size
Calibration segment selection bias: shorter segments may be systematically different
control_variables: Physiological state labels per segment
Signal quality metrics per segment
Explicit modeling of segment-length-dependent quantile estimation error (bootstrap)
Hierarchical/Bayesian conformal methods that pool information across segments
boring_rival_explanations: Short segments have worse coverage because they occur during physiologically unstable periods (transitions, artifacts), not because of finite-sample quantile estimation error
Segment length is a proxy for signal quality: event-triggered recordings capture brief clean epochs; coverage fails due to signal quality, not sample size
The model is misspecified for certain physiological regimes that happen to produce shorter segments; coverage fails due to misspecification, not finite-sample effects
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If finite-sample effects drive coverage instability, then coverage variance will scale as √(DoF/n_seg) even when segments are randomly subsampled from a stationary process; if physiological confounding drives it, coverage variance will correlate with state/quality metrics after controlling for n_seg.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a stationary physiological signal (e.g., resting ECG during stable sleep), randomly subsampled segments of varying lengths show coverage variance scaling as √(DoF/n_seg) with no residual correlation with any physiological metric; in real heterogeneous data, this scaling explains < 50% of coverage variance.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Requires separating statistical finite-sample effects from physiological confounding. Best tested by subsampling experiments on known-stationary data vs. real heterogeneous data.

possible_confounders: Covariate shift: morphology distribution changes across segments, but model error is independent of morphology (coverage fails due to covariate shift, not morphology-dependent misspecification)
Unmeasured hemodynamic variables (e.g., vascular resistance, compliance) driving both morphology and target, creating spurious morphology-error correlation
Sensor-specific morphology differences (e.g., wrist vs. finger PPG) confounded with subject groups
Calibration set morphology distribution not representative of deployment distribution (dataset shift)
control_variables: Simultaneous reference waveforms (tonometry, arterial line) for morphology validation
Vascular tone interventions (cold pressor, nitroglycerin, tilt table) to induce controlled morphology shifts
Multi-site PPG recordings to separate sensor-specific from physiological morphology variation
Explicit morphology features as covariates in conformal predictor
boring_rival_explanations: Coverage fails because the test morphology distribution shifts outside the calibration support (covariate shift), not because model error depends on morphology per se
Unmeasured hemodynamic state (e.g., vascular resistance) drives both morphology and BP; model error correlates with morphology only because both correlate with the true driver
Sensor placement differences (wrist vs. finger) create morphology differences that correlate with subject cohorts; coverage fails due to sensor-specific calibration, not morphology-dependent error
confounder_rival_builds.rival_prediction: If covariate shift drives coverage failure, then importance-weighted conformal prediction (weighting calibration by test morphology density) will restore nominal coverage without adding morphology as a covariate; if morphology-dependent misspecification drives it, importance weighting will fail but morphology-stratified conformal will succeed.
confounder_rival_builds.distinguishing_condition: In a dataset with induced morphology shifts (vascular interventions), importance-weighted conformal prediction using morphology density ratios achieves coverage within 3% of nominal across all shift magnitudes, while standard conformal shows > 10% deviation; morphology-stratified conformal also works but is not necessary.
confounder_rival_builds.confounder_rival_notes: Critical distinction: covariate shift vs. concept shift (morphology-dependent error). Testable via vascular interventions that shift morphology while monitoring reference hemodynamics, comparing importance weighting vs. stratification.
